title: Are commercial cleaning companies licensed?
answer: Commercial cleaning companies may need business licenses, registrations and other credentials depending on where they operate and the work they perform. In California, covered janitorial employers must register with the Labor Commissioner, which is different from a general business license.
sections: Understand which credential you are checking

The word licensed can hide several different questions. A business registration identifies the company, while a janitorial registration addresses a particular California employment requirement. Neither automatically proves that a provider is qualified for every specialized task. Ask for the legal business name and the credentials relevant to the proposed work, then check the issuing authority rather than relying on a logo or a statement in an advertisement.
Match documentation to the service

An office cleaning agreement should identify the actual provider responsible for the property. Insurance documentation should be current and consistent with that business identity. Work involving a separate regulated trade may require additional qualifications. Do not assume routine janitorial credentials authorize repairs, electrical work or specialized remediation. If those services are proposed, request a clear explanation of who will perform them and which requirements apply.
Make verification practical

Before granting access, confirm that documents belong to the company submitting the proposal. A difference between the marketing name and legal name can be legitimate, but it should be explained. Keep current records with your vendor information and revisit them when the agreement renews. This creates a stronger basis for hiring than accepting the broad phrase fully licensed without understanding what it means.
Verify the business, not just a badge

Registration status, insurance and relevant qualifications answer different concerns. A registration entry can help establish whether the legal business is recorded with the appropriate program, while insurance information addresses a separate contractual issue. Ask the provider to explain any difference between its legal and trading names. A screenshot or certificate with an old date should not be treated as a permanent record of current standing.

A useful vendor file records the company identity and the documents your property actually requires. If the provider changes its business entity, the old records may no longer describe the contracting company. Review changes at renewal or when notified, rather than assuming the first verification remains correct forever.

title: Can a cleaning company provide references?
answer: A cleaning company can provide client references when those clients have agreed to be contacted. The most useful references come from properties with service needs similar to yours and can describe reliability, communication and the quality of ongoing work.
sections: Choose references that fit your property

A reference from a small storefront may not answer the questions of a manager responsible for several occupied office floors. Look for similarities in building use, cleaning frequency and access requirements. You do not need an identical property, but you need enough context to understand the experience. Ask how long the client has used the provider and whether the reference concerns recurring service or a single project.
Ask about everyday performance

A polished testimonial rarely explains what happens after a missed area or an unexpected schedule change. A reference conversation can address whether visits were dependable, concerns reached the right person and corrections actually happened. Keep the discussion focused on the service rather than confidential business information. Specific examples are more useful than a general statement that the team was great.
Evaluate references alongside other evidence

References are one part of evaluating a cleaning provider. They do not replace a clear agreement, current documentation or an understanding of your own building. A company may also have privacy limits on sharing client names. Consider an authorized reference conversation or a relevant project description rather than pressuring the provider to disclose clients without permission.
Make reference conversations specific

Ask a reference about one relevant concern at a time. For example, a property with evening access can ask whether authorized entry was dependable, while a busy office can ask whether restrooms remained within the agreed standard. A reference who used only a one time project cannot necessarily describe months of recurring service. Keep the distinction visible when comparing providers.

Notice whether the reference can explain a problem and how it was handled. A service relationship with a corrected issue can be more informative than a vague claim that nothing ever went wrong. Do not request another client's rates, access information or confidential records. The conversation should establish experience relevant to your property, not expose someone else's business.

title: Do cleaning companies bring their own supplies?
answer: Many commercial cleaning companies bring the cleaning products and equipment needed for their agreed tasks. Restroom paper, soap, liners and other building consumables may be supplied by the property or the provider, so those responsibilities should be confirmed before service starts.
sections: Separate tools from building consumables

A vacuum, mop and cleaning solution serve the cleaning process. Toilet tissue and hand soap are supplies occupants use throughout the day. A proposal that includes cleaning supplies may cover the first group without covering the second. Name the items rather than assuming the phrase supplies includes everything in a restroom or break room. Also confirm compatibility with existing dispensers.
Account for property requirements

Some offices restrict fragrance, require particular surface care products or have limited storage. Share those requirements before the provider selects materials for the job. Specialty finishes and equipment can require manufacturer approved care. A product suitable for one surface is not automatically suitable for another, even when both are in the same room. The agreement should explain how property restrictions will be respected.
Avoid interruptions caused by missing items

Decide who notices low stock and who authorizes replenishment. Cleaning can be completed while a dispenser remains empty if nobody owns the restocking responsibility. Clarify where approved supplies are stored and whether the crew may access them. If the building supplies an item, it should be available when the crew arrives rather than locked away without an authorized contact.
Resolve supply exceptions before they interrupt service

Specialty dispensers, finish restrictions and storage limitations are common reasons a standard supply assumption fails. A building may already have a required soap cartridge or a floor product approved by its manufacturer. Tell the provider about these conditions before arrival so it can confirm whether the proposed arrangement works.

Ask what happens if approved stock is missing or a product restriction makes a task unavailable. The useful response is communication and an agreed alternative, not an improvised chemical choice. A cleaner should not have to guess whether a bottle left in a cupboard is approved for the surface or whether an occupant's personal product belongs to the building.

title: Do cleaning companies do background checks?
answer: Some cleaning companies conduct background checks, but screening practices vary by provider and assignment. Before granting access to an office, ask what screening is performed, which personnel it covers and how the company manages replacements and subcontractors.
sections: Ask what screened actually means

The phrase background checked does not identify the scope, timing or personnel covered. Ask the provider to describe its screening policy at a level appropriate for a customer. You generally need confirmation of the process rather than private employee records. A broad marketing promise should not substitute for an explanation of how the company decides who may work at your property.
Connect screening to access controls

Screening is only one part of protecting an occupied office. Restricted rooms, keys, alarm information and authorized work areas still need clear limits. Consider whether the crew will work with staff present or enter after everyone leaves. Your own access requirements should be shared before service begins so the provider can confirm whether it can meet them.
Include replacement personnel

A familiar crew member can be absent, and a building may require temporary coverage. Ask whether replacement personnel meet the same agreed requirements and how changes are communicated. If subcontractors are used, understand who verifies their eligibility and supervises their work. Consistency in these arrangements matters more than treating the first scheduled crew as the only people who will ever enter.
Screening does not replace site boundaries

Even when a company confirms screening, confidential documents should remain secured and restricted areas should remain clearly identified. Screening describes a personnel process; it does not determine which tenant room a worker is authorized to enter. Ask the provider to confirm how your requirements apply to everyone assigned to the property, including temporary coverage.

Avoid requesting sensitive personal records merely to prove that a policy exists. A customer level confirmation can explain the arrangement without revealing an individual worker's private history. If your organization has a formal vendor access requirement, share it before contracting so the company can determine whether it can meet that requirement.

title: Do you use employees or subcontractors?
answer: Cleaning companies may use employees, subcontractors or a combination, so the staffing arrangement should be confirmed with the provider. What matters to the customer is who performs the work, who supervises it and which company is accountable if a concern occurs.
sections: Understand who is responsible

The staffing label alone does not tell you whether cleaning will be dependable. A company using employees can still have weak supervision, while an arrangement involving subcontractors can have clear accountability. Ask who holds the service agreement and who handles concerns, access instructions and corrections. The customer should not need to track down an unfamiliar worker to resolve a problem.
Check consistency across the arrangement

If another company will enter your office, confirm how its work fits the agreement. Relevant documentation, screening requirements and property instructions should not disappear when the provider delegates an assignment. Ask whether subcontracting is permitted under your building rules and whether changes require notice. Plan for communication and coverage

The useful test is what happens when the regular worker is absent or an area is missed. There should be an identified contact who can coordinate a response and understand your scope. Avoid assumptions about staffing quality

Employee status does not automatically mean a person has been trained for your building, and subcontractor status does not automatically mean a person lacks supervision. Evaluate the actual responsibilities and communication chain. The relevant concern is whether the contracting provider remains accountable for the promised work and the people it authorizes to enter.

title: Do you use green cleaning products?

An office with fragrance sensitivities may have different requirements from a property following a formal environmental purchasing standard. Ask which products will be used on which surfaces and whether alternatives are available for restricted areas.
Distinguish certification from advertising

EPA Safer Choice offers a searchable list of products meeting its standard. That provides a more concrete reference than a bottle described only as eco friendly. Review the intended use and manufacturer directions alongside the environmental claim.
Keep performance and compatibility in view

A cleaning program needs to remove the soil present without creating avoidable problems for occupants or surfaces. title: How do cleaning companies inspect work quality?
answer: Cleaning companies can inspect work quality by comparing completed tasks with the agreed scope and checking whether concerns have been corrected. sections: Start with an agreed result

An inspection is meaningful only when both sides understand what was included. Empty bins, serviced restrooms and clean accessible surfaces are different commitments from specialty floor restoration or interior window work. A bright lobby does not prove every required room was covered. Clear expectations allow a manager to distinguish a missed task from work that was never part of the agreement.
Look for patterns rather than isolated impressions

A single visit may reveal a problem, but recurring concerns help identify whether the service arrangement needs adjustment. Record the location and nature of the issue so the provider can respond precisely. A room used heavily after the cleaning visit can look different by morning. Consider when the inspection occurs and what happened between completion and review.
Evaluate how corrections are handled

The most useful quality process closes the loop. Ask who receives a concern, how the provider confirms the relevant work and how the customer learns what happened. Inspections should support consistent service rather than become paperwork nobody uses. A repeated missed area deserves a clear response and an explanation of whether access, scope or performance caused the problem.
Know what an inspection can tell you

A visual check can identify missed soil, but a spotless looking room does not by itself establish every hygiene claim. Evaluate tasks using the agreed purpose and appropriate evidence. Do not interpret a polished surface as a laboratory finding or demand that routine cleaners prove an unsupported health guarantee.

For recurring concerns, describe the room, task and timing. A report that says the building is dirty gives the provider less useful information than identifying an unserviced bin in a specified room. Good customer communication makes the issue assessable without publishing the company's internal inspection checklist or scoring system.

title: How do you handle keys, fobs, and alarm codes?
answer: Keys, fobs and alarm codes should be shared only through an agreed access arrangement with authorized cleaning personnel. The property and provider should confirm who may enter, which areas are permitted and how access is returned or changed when service ends.

A cleaner does not need unrestricted access simply because service takes place after hours. Identify the rooms included, the doors used and any spaces that remain off limits. Separate instructions for shared areas from instructions for confidential offices. Protect access information

Do not place alarm details in a public article, a visible note or a broadly shared message. Use the communication method agreed with the provider and your security contact. Ask how the company confirms which people are authorized for the assignment. Access arrangements should also address the situation in which a fob fails or an alarm does not behave as expected.
Plan for changes and service completion

Staffing and tenancy can change. Explain who must be notified before another person enters and who can authorize replacement access. When the agreement ends, confirm return of physical items and coordinate changes to electronic permissions with the property team. A clear handoff prevents old access from remaining active simply because nobody owned the final step.
Treat access changes as a property decision

A new tenant, a changed alarm arrangement or a replaced lock can affect a cleaning visit even if the written tasks remain unchanged. Keep the authorized property contact involved so the provider receives current instructions. A crew should not be expected to bypass a locked door or seek access information from an unrelated occupant.

title: How often should an office be professionally cleaned?
answer: An office should be professionally cleaned often enough to match its occupancy, restroom use, food activity and visible soil. Busy shared spaces may need more frequent attention than lightly used private offices, so the schedule should reflect how the building is actually used.
sections: Look beyond square footage

Two offices of the same size can create very different cleaning needs. A staff of several people working occasional days does not use restrooms and break rooms like a busy office receiving visitors throughout the week. Consider which rooms remain occupied, where food is consumed and how quickly bins fill. The service schedule should reflect these conditions rather than copy another building's timetable.
Give shared spaces appropriate attention

Restrooms, kitchens and entrances often reveal whether the schedule is keeping up with use. A lobby may look acceptable while soap dispensers run empty or food residue remains in a break room. Separate the needs of individual zones instead of applying one uniform assumption to every surface. Periodic detail work can also be planned separately from recurring cleaning.
Adjust when building use changes

A new tenant, an expanded staff or a return to regular office attendance can make an old schedule inadequate. Review the condition between visits and discuss repeated concerns with the provider. The objective is a workable program, not cleaning more often without a reason. If problems consistently appear well before the next visit, the scope or timing may need attention.
Separate demand from appearance alone

An office with hybrid attendance may look quiet while a shared restroom or break room receives concentrated use. Conversely, a large room that remains unused may not need the same visit frequency as a small occupied kitchen. Consider the condition of each shared area and the responsibilities already handled by staff.

Repeated shortages or soil between visits can reflect a scope gap rather than poor performance during the last appointment. Discuss whether the provider is being asked to maintain occupied conditions while only being present after hours. Choose the arrangement that fits the building

A small office may need a limited recurring scope, while a larger building may require coordinated service across several shared areas. That is more informative than debating which term sounds more professional.

Create a clear comparison using the rooms, recurring tasks and service periods each provider describes. Ask for clarification wherever a term could represent several different scopes.
